hints: Start by thinking about what holds the two strands of a DNA double helix together, and what very high heat close to boiling will do to those weak bonds.
Next think about why the mixture is cooled to $50 ^\circ\text{C}$ - what small DNA pieces are in the tube and what do they need to do before new DNA can be made.
Finally think about what Taq polymerase does best at its optimum of $72 ^\circ\text{C}$ using free deoxynucleotides to build on the primers.
walkthrough:
Breaking Open the Double Helix at 95 Degrees**
Think of DNA as a ladder held together by many weak hydrogen bonds between bases. At $95 ^\circ\text{C}$ there is so much kinetic energy that these hydrogen bonds break. The double-stranded DNA denatures into two separate single strands, and each single strand can now act as a template.

Attaching the Start Signals at 50 Degrees**
DNA polymerase cannot start from nothing, it needs a short starter called a primer. Cooling to $50 ^\circ\text{C}$ lets the primers form hydrogen bonds with their complementary sequences on the single-stranded template DNA. This is annealing, and it marks exactly where copying will begin.

Building the New Strand at 72 Degrees**
$72 ^\circ\text{C}$ is close to the optimum temperature for Taq polymerase from hot-spring bacteria. The enzyme adds free deoxynucleotides complementary to the template, extending from the primers to make a second strand. Each single template becomes double-stranded again, so DNA is doubled each cycle.

Final answer: At $95 ^\circ\text{C}$ DNA denatures as hydrogen bonds break and double-stranded DNA separates into single strands; at $50 ^\circ\text{C}$ primers anneal / bind to complementary sequences on single-stranded DNA; at $72 ^\circ\text{C}$ Taq polymerase synthesises a complementary second strand to form double-stranded DNA.

hints: Look carefully at Fig. 5.1 and the habitat notes - where can alpine plants live on South, Stewart and North Islands, and where can lowland plants live continuously?
Think about what sea water between South Island and Stewart Island, and lowland forest valleys between mountain tops, do to movement of pollen and seeds.
Contrast this with M. pottsiana on North Island, where lowland habitat is mostly continuous with no sea or mountain barrier inside the island.
Recall what happens to random mutations and allele frequencies when populations can no longer exchange genes and experience different environments.
Link this pattern of divergence with a geographical barrier to the named type of speciation that could be starting.
walkthrough:
Seeing the Barriers on the Map**
Alpine Myosotis can only live above the tree line on mountain tops. South Island and Stewart Island both have alpine tops but they are separated by sea. Different mountains on South Island are separated by lowland valleys where alpine plants cannot grow. Lowland M. pottsiana on North Island lives in mostly continuous lowland habitat with no such internal barrier.

No Gene Flow for the Alpine Species**
Pollen and seeds of M. pygmaea rarely cross the sea, and pollen and seeds of M. pulvinaris rarely cross the valleys between peaks. That means almost no interbreeding and no exchange of alleles between populations. Each population has its own closed gene pool.

Populations Diverge Genetically**
In isolation, random different mutations arise in each population. Different mountain or island environments mean different selection pressures, for example cold, wind, soil and pollinators. Natural selection and genetic drift therefore change allele frequencies in different directions, producing the observed genetic differences.

Naming the Process and Explaining the Contrast**
Divergence driven by a geographical barrier is the start of allopatric speciation. If it continues, populations may become reproductively isolated even if they meet again. M. pottsiana shows the opposite: continuous habitat allows interbreeding and gene flow, similar environments give similar selection pressures, so alleles stay mixed and populations remain genetically similar.

Final answer: M. pygmaea populations on South Island and Stewart Island are geographically isolated by sea and M. pulvinaris populations on different South Island mountain tops are isolated by unsuitable lowland habitat, so there is little or no interbreeding / gene flow between populations. Different mutations occur randomly and different selection pressures / environments act, leading to different changes in allele frequencies / gene pools, so allopatric speciation may be occurring. In contrast, M. pottsiana has no geographical isolation within continuous lowland North Island, so gene flow / interbreeding continues under similar selection pressures, maintaining genetic similarity.

hints: Think beyond selection to random chance - what happens to allele frequencies when a population becomes very small or is started by just a few seeds on a new island.
Think about other ways alleles are added, removed or favoured - movement of individuals between populations, brand new alleles, or human choice by gardeners and breeders.
walkthrough:
Random and Introduced Changes**
Natural selection is only one driver. In small island populations, chance alone can change allele frequencies. This is genetic drift, including a bottleneck when numbers crash or a founder effect when a new population is started by few individuals. Migration moves alleles between populations by pollen or seed dispersal, increasing or homogenising variation.

New Alleles and Human Selection**
Mutation creates entirely new alleles by changes in DNA sequence, the ultimate source of genetic variation. Humans can also drive rapid change by artificial selection, selectively breeding plants with desired flower or growth traits, which changes allele frequencies in cultivated Myosotis.
Final answer: Any two from: genetic drift / genetic bottleneck / founder effect; migration / gene flow; mutation; artificial selection / selective breeding.
